review.notes: Built on the course: data types, DIKW, quality dimensions, mean vs median, range, percent vs points, growth, CAGR, real growth, volume check, chart choice, truncated axes, lie factor, cherry-picking, correlation vs causation, sample bias. Calculations checked. Fictional company.

content.company: Harborview Retail (fictional), a chain of 40 grocery stores
content.briefing: The board meets on Thursday. You must check the board pack: numbers, growth claims, charts and conclusions. Your manager wants every claim to survive tough questions.

variants.text: Five orders this morning: Kz 10 k, 12 k, 13 k, 15 k and 150 k. Which average describes a typical order?

choices.f: One big order skews the mean to Kz 40 k. The median shows the typical order.
The mean is pulled up by one outlier.
Each value occurs once. The mode does not help here.

variants.text: Customer satisfaction is recorded as 'poor, fair, good, excellent'. What type of data is this?

choices.f: Categories with a natural order. Use the median or mode, not the mean.
They are labels, not measured numbers.
Nominal categories have no order; these do.

variants.text: The sales file has the same invoice twice and some stores missing for March. Which quality dimensions fail?

choices.f: Duplicates break uniqueness; missing stores break completeness.
Two different dimensions fail here.
The data may be on time and still flawed.

variants.text: A store manager says: 'We sold 4,000 units.' What turns this into information?

choices.f: Data plus context is information. DIKW starts here.
Precision is not context.

choices.t: A bigger font on the slide
choices.f: Presentation does not add meaning.

variants.text: Market share rose from 20% to 25%. How should the board pack describe it?

choices.f: Both are true; points avoid confusion.
That mixes points and percent. Relative growth is 25%.
Share moved 5 points, not 25.

variants.text: Sales rose from Kz 40 m to Kz 46 m. What is the growth rate?

choices.f: 6 is the change in millions, not a rate.
That divides by the new value. Divide by the old.

variants.text: Revenue grew from Kz 100 m to Kz 133.1 m over 3 years. What is the CAGR?

choices.f: That divides 33.1% by 3, ignoring compounding.
That is total growth, not the yearly rate.

variants.text: Nominal sales growth is 25%; inflation is 20%. What is real growth?

choices.f: Subtraction is close but not exact. Use the ratio.
That ignores inflation.

variants.text: Sales value is up 18%, but cases sold are down 6%. What do you tell the board?

choices.t: Growth is price, not more volume
choices.f: The volume check shows fewer cases at higher prices.
Customers are buying less. Value hides it.

choices.t: The case data must be wrong
choices.f: Worth checking, but price inflation explains it well.

variants.text: Sales in Kz rose 30% last year, while inflation was 28%. How do you describe it?

choices.t: Real growth was close to zero

choices.f: Most of it is inflation.
Real growth is slightly positive.

variants.text: You want to show monthly sales over the last 24 months. Which chart?

choices.f: Trends over time read best as lines.
Pies show parts of a whole, not trends.
3D distorts values and hides the trend.

variants.text: To compare sales across 8 stores this month, which chart?

choices.f: Bars compare categories; sorting shows ranking.
Lines imply a sequence over time.
Hard to compare similar slices.

variants.text: A bar chart's axis starts at 95. Store A's 98 bar looks three times store B's 96. What is wrong?

choices.f: The truncated axis exaggerates a 2% difference.
It misleads readers about size.
3D makes distortion worse.

variants.text: Sales rose 10%, but the chart's bars grew 50% in height. What is the lie factor?

choices.f: Effect shown 50% / effect in data 10%. Far from 1 = misleading.
You divided the wrong way.
That subtracts instead of dividing.

variants.text: Stores with more staff have higher sales. The pack concludes: 'Hire more staff to raise sales.' What do you say?

choices.f: Bigger stores have more staff and more sales. Store size is a third cause.
Moving together does not prove one causes the other.
Staff may matter, but this data cannot prove it.

variants.text: How could you test whether more staff raises sales?

choices.t: A test against a control group
choices.f: A controlled test separates cause from coincidence.

choices.t: Ask store managers if they agree
choices.f: Opinions are not evidence of cause.

choices.t: Study the same chart once again
choices.f: More looking does not test causation.

variants.text: A study of 'our 10 best stores' finds they all have loyalty cards, so cards must work.

choices.t: Survivorship bias: check stores that failed too
choices.f: Closed stores also had cards. The sample hid them.
Only successes were studied.

choices.t: A sample of 10 is always enough
choices.f: Size is not the main issue; selection is.

variants.text: The pack shows sales from the low point in April to the peak in November only.

choices.t: Cherry-picked dates: show the full year
choices.f: Chosen start and end points exaggerate growth.
It hides the earlier decline.
Precision does not fix selection.

variants.text: A dashboard tile reads '87%' with no label, period or target. What do you ask for?

choices.f: Without context, 87% means nothing.

choices.t: A brighter colour for the tile
choices.f: Colour adds no meaning.
Precision without context is still unclear.

variants.text: The board wants one number that tells them if stores are doing well.

choices.t: A key measure against target and last year
choices.f: Comparison gives the number meaning.
Without comparison, it cannot say 'well'.
Activity without value or target.
